books.title: Animals, Animals
books.art_why: Real animals such as elk, giraffes, elephants, and foxes can be photographed.

pages.text: There are many kinds of animals. The elk is in the deer family. Male elk have large antlers. Elk can swim well and run very fast. on their heads. and short horns all over their bodies Giraffes have spots with long necks. Giraffes are very tall.
pages.brief: Many animals appear together. A male elk in the deer family has large antlers and stands near water; elk can swim well and run very fast. A very tall giraffe with a long neck and spots stands nearby.

pages.text: Elephants are the largest land animals. Elephants have long trunks. They live in grasslands and forests. They have thick fur to keep them warm. Snow leopards live on cold mountains.
pages.brief: An elephant, the largest land animal, stands among grasslands and forests, with a very long trunk hanging down. High on a cold mountain, a snow leopard rests, with thick fur to keep it very warm.

pages.text: This camel has a long winter coat. Camels can live for a long time without food or water. Foxes eat small animals, insects, fruits, and eggs. Foxes live in holes in the ground. The fox is in the dog family.
pages.brief: A camel with a long winter coat stands; camels can live for a long time without food or water. A fox in the dog family stands by a hole in the ground where foxes live.

pages.text: The zebra is in the horse family. Zebras have white and black stripes and live in grasslands. The hair on their necks stands straight up. Kangaroos eat grass and other plants. It uses its strong back legs to hop. The great gray kangaroo has a pouch.
pages.brief: A zebra with white and black stripes stands in grasslands; the hair on its neck stands straight up. A great gray kangaroo with a pouch uses strong back legs to hop while eating grass and plants.

pages.text: The hippopotamus spends most of its time in water. A hippopotamus has almost no hair. It eats grass and water plants. There are many kinds of animals. They eat seals, birds, and fish. They have thick fur to stay warm. Polar bears live in cold places.
pages.brief: A hippopotamus spends most of its time in water, with almost no hair, eating grass and water plants. In a cold place, a polar bear with very thick fur stands near seals, birds, and fish.

books.title: Weird Bird Beaks
books.art_why: Real birds and their beaks can be photographed today.

pages.text: Crossbill My beak is crossed like an X. My beak gets the seeds out of tree cones. I use it to knock down fruit. I have a horn on top of my beak. Rhinoceros Hornbill.
pages.brief: A Crossbill is shown in a tree, its crossed X-shaped beak reaching into a tree cone to pull out seeds, while it also knocks down fruit. A Rhinoceros Hornbill is shown nearby with a horn on top of its beak.

pages.text: Sword-Billed Hummingbird I use my long beak to drink from flowers. I can hold fish in the skin under my beak. Brown Pelican.
pages.brief: A Sword-Billed Hummingbird is at a flower, reaching its long beak in to drink. A Brown Pelican is shown with fish held in the loose skin under its beak. Both birds are shown so their beaks can be clearly seen.

pages.text: Shoebill Stork My beak is shaped like a shoe. My long beak looks like a spoon. Spoonbill.
pages.brief: A Shoebill Stork stands with its large beak shaped like a shoe. A Spoonbill stands beside it, its long beak looking like a spoon. Both birds are shown facing forward so their beak shapes stand out.

pages.text: Toucan My huge and colorful beak is very light. Which beak is your favorite? Many birds have weird beaks.
pages.brief: A Toucan is shown with a huge, colorful beak that looks very light. Around it are many other birds with weird beaks, all shown together so their different beak shapes can be compared. The Toucan stands out among them with its own unusual beak.

books.title: Summer Olympic Events
books.art_why: The book describes real Summer Olympic sports and athletes today, which can be photographed.

pages.text: The Summer Olympic Games The Summer Olympics are held every four years. They are held in cities around the world.
pages.brief: A wide view of a host city with a large Summer Olympic venue, showing that the Summer Olympic Games are held every four years in cities around the world. The scene focuses on the city setting and the place where the Games take place.

pages.text: Let’s look at some of the games.
pages.brief: A group of Summer Olympic athletes in a sports setting, ready to show some of the games. The view introduces the different events that will be looked at, with athletes present as the page turns to specific sports.

pages.text: Water Sports There are many water sports. One water sport is swimming.
pages.brief: Swimmers in water during a Summer Olympic swimming event, showing one of the many water sports. The athletes are moving through the water in a pool setting, making clear that swimming is a water sport at the Games.

pages.text: Some swimming races use only one kind of stroke. Other races use many strokes.
pages.brief: Swimmers using different strokes in Summer Olympic swimming races. Some swimmers use only one kind of stroke, while others use many strokes as they move through the water. The pool setting shows the races taking place.

pages.text: Another water sport is diving. Divers jump from high above the water.
pages.brief: A diver jumping from a high diving board above the water at a Summer Olympic water sport event. The diver is in the air, high above the pool, showing that divers jump from high above the water.

pages.text: Track and Field Track and field events are games of running, throwing, and jumping. Races can be short or long. Summer Olympic Events.
pages.brief: Track and field athletes at a Summer Olympic venue, taking part in running, throwing, and jumping events. Some run in short races and some run in long races on the track, showing games of running, throwing, and jumping.

pages.text: In throwing games, people win by throwing objects the farthest.
pages.brief: Track and field athletes in a throwing game at the Summer Olympics. A person throws an object as far as possible while competing to win by throwing the farthest, with the field setting showing the throwing event.

pages.text: In the high jump, people leap over In the long jump, people leap as far as they can. Summer Olympic Events.
pages.brief: Two track and field jumping events at the Summer Olympics. One athlete leaps over a high bar in the high jump, and another leaps as far as possible in the long jump, both in a field setting.

pages.text: Gymnastics Gymnasts leap, flip, and twirl. They need strength, skill, and good timing.
pages.brief: Gymnasts leaping, flipping, and twirling in a Summer Olympic gymnastics setting. They show strength, skill, and good timing as they perform their moves during competition. The gym setting focuses on the gymnasts and their active, skillful routines.

pages.text: Gymnasts compete on the balance beam. They must balance on the beam while they turn and flip. Summer Olympic Events.
pages.brief: A gymnast competing on the balance beam at a Summer Olympic gymnastics event. The gymnast must balance on the beam while turning and flipping, with the beam and gym setting showing this gymnastics event. The athlete is shown on the beam, turning and flipping while keeping balance.

pages.text: Gymnasts compete on the rings. They hold onto the rings and flip their bodies in circles.
pages.brief: A gymnast competing on the rings at a Summer Olympic gymnastics event. The gymnast holds onto the rings and flips their body in circles, with the rings and gym setting showing this gymnastics event. The athlete’s body is in motion as they hold on and turn.

pages.text: The Summer Olympics include many sports. Which sports do you like? Summer Olympic Sports Summer Olympic Events.
pages.brief: A wide view of several Summer Olympic sports, with athletes from different events together. The scene shows that the Summer Olympics include many sports, inviting viewers to think about which sports they like. The athletes are shown in their sports settings.

books.title: Legs, Wings, Fins, and Flippers
books.art_why: All the animals shown are real living species that can be photographed today.

pages.text: Legs, Wings, Fins, and Flippers.
pages.brief: An opening nature scene showing a few real animals together: a four-legged animal standing on its legs, a bird holding its wings open, and a fish with fins and a tail in water, bringing together the four kinds of animal body parts named in the title.

pages.text: Introduction Animals move in many ways. Animals have different body parts to help them move.
pages.brief: A wide outdoor view of several different animals moving at the same time in their own ways: one animal walking on legs across the ground, one bird flying with wings above it, and one fish swimming through water with fins and tail, showing that animals move in many ways.

pages.text: On Land Most animals that live on land have legs. Animals can have different numbers of legs.
pages.brief: A group of land animals photographed on the ground, each standing or walking on a different number of legs: a two-legged bird, a four-legged dog, a six-legged insect on a leaf, and an eight-legged spider on its web, showing that animals can have different numbers of legs.

pages.text: Horses have long legs to run fast. Frogs have long back legs to leap.
pages.brief: A horse with long legs galloping fast across an open field, and beside it a frog with long back legs pushing off to leap from a pond edge, both animals using their legs to move quickly over land.

pages.text: Some animals have no legs. These animals slide their bodies to move.
pages.brief: Legless animals moving along the ground: a snake sliding its long body forward over dry earth and a worm stretching and pulling itself through soft soil, both using their bodies instead of legs to move.

pages.text: Do You Know? Flying squirrels do not really fly. They glide, or fall slowly. In the Air Birds, bats, and many insects use wings to fly. Animals can have two wings or four wings.
pages.brief: A flying squirrel spreading the skin between its outstretched limbs to glide down from a tree branch, while nearby a bird flaps its wings, a bat flies with leathery wings, and insects with two and four wings hover in the air.

pages.text: Chicks can’t fly until they grow strong feathers.
pages.brief: A young chick standing on the ground with small fluffy downy wings held out from its sides, not yet able to fly, waiting as its strong adult feathers have not grown in yet.

pages.text: Animal wings come in many shapes and sizes.
pages.brief: A close comparison of animal wings of different shapes and sizes: a wide spotted butterfly wing, a bat's long leathery wing, and a bird's broad feathered wing, all shown side by side so their differences are easy to see.

pages.text: In Water Fish use fins and tails to move through the water.
pages.brief: Underwater view of fish moving through clear water, their fins spread out on their sides and backs and their tails sweeping from side to side to push them forward through the water.

pages.text: Whales have fins and flippers. But seals, sea lions, and sea turtles only have flippers.
pages.brief: A whale swimming with its fins and flippers visible in the water, and nearby a seal, a sea lion and a sea turtle, each moving through the sea using only its flippers.

pages.text: Penguins are birds, but they have flippers instead of wings. Penguins swim to hunt fish in the ocean. On land, they can walk, or they can slide on their bellies.
pages.brief: Penguins in the ocean swimming with their flippers to hunt fish, and the same penguins on land walking upright or sliding along on their bellies over the ice, showing their flippers instead of wings.

pages.text: Some animals that live in water have webbed feet. Webbed feet help animals swim better.
pages.brief: A close look at webbed feet in water: a duck's foot with skin stretched between the toes paddling below the surface, and a frog's webbed back foot spread out as it swims, both helping the animal move better through water.

pages.text: Conclusion Watch how animals move in the world around you. Think about the body parts that help animals move. Think about how you move, too!
pages.brief: A child outdoors watching real animals moving around them — a bird overhead, an animal on legs nearby, a fish in a pond — while thinking about the body parts that help each animal move, and about how the child moves too.

books.title: Goats Are Great!
books.art_why: Goats are real animals that live today, so real photographs suit every page.

pages.text: Goats Are Great!
pages.brief: A small group of goats standing together in a green sunny field, heads lifted toward the viewer, with a wooden fence and rolling hills behind them. Soft morning light on their coats, a few goats close to the front and others further back, calm and alert.

pages.text: What’s so great about goats? Goats give us food. They help us and play with us. Goats make great pets.
pages.brief: A child sitting on grass beside a friendly goat, one hand resting on its back, both outdoors in a grassy yard. Nearby a glass of milk and a small bowl of cheese sit on a low wooden table, showing the food goats give, and the goat leans in close and calm.

pages.text: Goats provide food for us. Many people drink goat milk. Goat milk makes goat cheese! Some people eat goat meat.
pages.brief: A kitchen table showing a glass of white goat milk, a round of fresh white goat cheese, and a covered dish. A pair of hands pours milk from a jug, and in the background a goat stands at an open doorway looking in, outdoors beyond.

pages.text: Goats help us in many ways. Goats are happy to eat weeds in people’s yards. We can make wool cloth out of soft goat hair.
pages.brief: A goat standing in a garden bed nibbling tall weeds, while a person in gloves holds a basket of pulled weeds nearby. In the foreground, a folded stack of soft woven cloth rests on a wooden bench, made from soft goat hair.

pages.text: Goats make great pets and are fun to play with. Goats learn to come when you call their name. Goats are easy to take care of.
pages.brief: A goat trotting toward a child who is crouching low with an outstretched hand, calling it across a grassy yard. The goat's ears lift and its head is forward, and behind them a simple pen with a water bucket shows easy care.

pages.text: Goats like to be outdoors. They enjoy sunny days. Goats spend most of their day playing and eating.
pages.brief: Several goats outdoors on a bright sunny day, some grazing on short grass and others lying down or nudging each other. Long shadows on the grass, a clear blue sky, and a low stone wall at the edge of the meadow.

pages.text: Goats are great to look at. Many have long, floppy ears. Goats have only lower teeth. All goats have two hard toes on each foot.
pages.brief: A close view of a goat's head with long floppy ears hanging down, its mouth open enough to show the lower front teeth. Below, a close look at one hoof with two hard toes resting on grass and small stones.

pages.text: Both boy and girl goats can have long beards. Some baby goats are born with tiny horns. Goat hair is very soft to touch.
pages.brief: Two goats side by side, one male and one female, both with long beards on their chins. A small baby goat stands in front with tiny budding horns, and a hand gently touches the soft hair on its back.

pages.text: Goats eat healthy foods. Goats like to eat long grass. They like flowers and apples. Goats eat anything yummy.
pages.brief: A goat with its head down in long grass, another nibbling bright flowers at the edge of a garden, and a third stretching up to reach apples on a low branch. Green grass and sunlight all around them.

pages.text: Goats are strong and quick. Goats like to climb and jump. They play king of the mountain!
pages.brief: Goats clambering up a rocky slope and a fallen log, one leaping from stone to stone while another stands high on the top rock. Dust and grass below, blue sky behind, the goats pushing and climbing together.

pages.text: Goats are smart, playful, gentle, and helpful. Goats are fun and friendly. That’s why goats are great!
pages.brief: A lively group of goats together in a sunny meadow, some jumping, one climbing a low rock, one nudging a child's hand. Bright grass, soft light, and the whole herd friendly and playful, filling the picture.

books.title: At a Touch Tank
books.art_why: Touch tank sea animals are real and can be photographed today.

pages.text: This touch tank has animals from the coast of Alaska. They live in very cold water.
pages.brief: A touch tank filled with very cold seawater holds animals from the coast of Alaska. Several small coastal sea creatures rest under the water inside the tank. The water looks clear and cold. The tank is the setting where these Alaskan coastal animals live.

pages.text: Sea stars live in this touch tank.
pages.brief: Sea stars rest inside the touch tank. Their arms spread out on the bottom and sides under the cold water. Several sea stars are visible in the tank, showing the shape of these coastal animals. The tank water surrounds them.

pages.text: This blood star is red like blood. It has five arms, like most sea stars. It feels rough when I touch it. Blood stars eat sponges and tiny ocean animals.
pages.brief: A blood star lies in the touch tank, its body red like blood and its five arms spread out. A hand gently touches its rough surface. Small sponges and tiny ocean animals are nearby in the water.

pages.text: Anemones live in this touch tank.
pages.brief: Anemones sit in the touch tank. Their soft bodies and tentacles are under the cold water. Several anemones are visible among the coastal animals inside the tank. The tank water surrounds them and holds them for touching.

pages.text: This anemone is pale pink. It has many soft tentacles. The tentacles gently grab my fingers when I touch them. Anemones eat little shrimp and fish.
pages.brief: A pale pink anemone sits in the touch tank. Many soft tentacles stretch out in the water. A hand's fingers gently touch the tentacles, and the tentacles gently grab them. Little shrimp and fish are nearby.

pages.text: Sea urchins live in this touch tank.
pages.brief: Sea urchins rest in the touch tank. Their round bodies and many spines are under the cold water. Several sea urchins are visible among the coastal animals inside the tank. The tank water surrounds them and keeps them in view.

pages.text: This red sea urchin has many long spines. The sharp spines move when I touch them. Red sea urchins eat seaweed and other ocean plants.
pages.brief: A red sea urchin sits in the touch tank with many long spines. A hand's fingers gently touch the sharp spines, and the spines move. Seaweed and other ocean plants grow nearby in the cold water around it.

pages.text: Sea cucumbers live in this touch tank.
pages.brief: Sea cucumbers rest in the touch tank. Their long bodies lie on the bottom under the cold water among the coastal animals. Several sea cucumbers are visible inside the tank. The tank water surrounds them.

pages.text: This sea cucumber is the color of a brick. Its body is covered with little bumps. The bumps look sharp, but they feel soft. Sea cucumbers eat tiny plants and animals in the ocean.
pages.brief: A sea cucumber lies in the touch tank, its body the color of a brick. Little bumps cover its body. A hand's fingers gently touch the bumps, which look sharp but feel soft. Tiny ocean plants and animals are nearby.

pages.text: I never poke, pull, squeeze, or move the animals. I touch all of them gently with just two fingers. I want all the animals to stay safe.
pages.brief: A child's hand with just two fingers gently touches the animals in the touch tank. The hand does not poke, pull, squeeze, or move them. The coastal animals stay safe in the cold water around the hand.

books.title: What Lives in This Hole?
books.art_why: All the animals and burrows are real and can be photographed today.

pages.text: Animal Burrows Many animals live in holes called burrows. I wanted to know more about them.
pages.brief: Open outdoor ground with several dark holes dug into the soil, burrow entrances set between grass roots and low plants. Small animals are near the openings, some slipping down into the holes, showing many different animals living in burrows.

pages.text: My teacher helped me learn about them. I used the computer to share Come see what I learned!
pages.brief: A teacher stands beside a child at a classroom computer, both looking at the screen while the child points at it. The child turns toward the viewer with an eager, proud expression, ready to show what was learned.

pages.text: Staying Cool A tortoise lives in this hole! It lives in a desert. It digs a burrow to get away from the heat.
pages.brief: A desert tortoise digs into sandy ground, front legs scooping soil, its body half inside a burrow entrance. Around it stretch dry cracked earth, scattered rocks and low desert plants under strong sunlight, the tortoise working to get away from the heat.

pages.text: Wowser! The goliath bird-eating spider is as big as a dinner plate. Keeping Eggs Safe A big spider lives in this hole! It lays eggs in a little bag. It takes the bag when it leaves to find food.
pages.brief: A goliath bird-eating spider, huge and hairy, sits at the mouth of its ground burrow, its leg span as wide as a dinner plate. It grips a small silk egg bag and carries it along as it moves off across the soil to find food.

pages.text: Making a Nest This is a hole for puffins! They spend most of their time at sea.
pages.brief: A puffin stands on grassy ground at the entrance of its burrow, black and white body, orange legs and feet, the open sea stretching away behind it. The bird is on land beside the hole, having come from the water where it spends most of its time.

pages.text: Wowser! Puffins may have bright colors on their bills. Some people call puffins “clowns of the sea.” The burrow is a nest. Both parents take care of the egg.
pages.brief: Two puffins at their burrow nest, bills bright with color, one standing at the entrance while the other crouches beside a single egg in the soft hollow inside. Both parent birds stay close, taking care of the egg together.

pages.text: Living in the Dark Naked mole rats live in this hole! They live in the dark.
pages.brief: Naked mole rats deep in a dark underground burrow, hairless pink wrinkled bodies clustered close together, one against the tunnel wall. Packed earth surrounds the passage and no daylight reaches them, the animals living in darkness.

pages.text: They dig tunnels to find food. One animal digs. Others move the dirt away.
pages.brief: Inside a narrow tunnel, one naked mole rat digs at the earth with its front teeth while two others push the loose soil back along the passage behind it. The group works in a line, moving dirt away from the digging.

pages.text: Hiding and Laying Eggs A big salamander lives in this underwater hole! It lives in rivers and streams. It hides all day and hunts at night.
pages.brief: A big salamander rests inside an underwater hole in a river bank, its body tucked into the dark opening with water flowing above it. Stones and stream bed surround the hole, the salamander hidden away during the day.

pages.text: The burrow is a safe place for eggs. A female lays many eggs. A male keeps the eggs safe.
pages.brief: Inside a damp burrow chamber, a female salamander sits beside a cluster of many eggs while a male salamander stays close, keeping watch over them. The eggs rest in a wet hollow of the burrow, safe in the dim space.

pages.text: Wowser! A wombat’s burrow may be as long as three school buses! Taking a Nap A wombat lives in this hole! It sleeps in its burrow all day. It comes out to find food at night.
pages.brief: A wombat sleeps curled inside a burrow tunnel that stretches far away into the earth. Outside at night, the same wombat stands on the open ground, nose down, out searching for food after sleeping all day.

pages.text: More to Come Other animals live in burrows, too. It is so fun to learn about animals!
pages.brief: Several animals sit at the mouths of their burrows on open outdoor ground, some small and some large, each near its own hole. The burrow openings spread across the scene, showing there are more animals to learn about.

books.title: Pocket Parks
books.art_why: Pocket parks are real places in cities today and can be photographed.

pages.text: What Is a Pocket Park? Some cities don’t have space for big, grassy parks. That’s why they build pocket parks instead.
pages.brief: Show a crowded city neighborhood with buildings and streets close together, leaving no space for a big, grassy park; show a small pocket park built into the city as the park people use instead.

pages.text: A pocket park is like a regular park, only smaller. A pocket park can take up a city block. It can also be as small as a parking space.
pages.brief: Show a small pocket park about the size of a city block, and beside it show an even smaller pocket park that is only as big as a parking space; both look like regular parks, only smaller.

pages.text: Lots of Empty Lots An empty lot is a great place for a pocket park. It can take many workers to build one.
pages.brief: Show an empty city lot with bare ground and no park yet, and show many workers building a pocket park there; they work together to turn the empty lot into a new small park for people.

pages.text: People who live close by can help, too. They can plant flowers or trees. They can also help keep the park clean and safe. Every pocket park is different.
pages.brief: Show people who live close by a pocket park in the city helping there: some plant flowers and trees, while others help keep the park clean and safe; make this park look different from other pocket parks.

pages.text: Different Pocket Parks This pocket park has a waterfall at the back. It also has many places for people to sit.
pages.brief: Show a pocket park inside the city with a waterfall at the back and many places for people to sit throughout the park, so visitors have moving water to look at and plenty of seating.

pages.text: Check out the colorful art at this pocket park. It has a swing to play on, too.
pages.brief: Show a pocket park inside the city with colorful art on display and a swing for people to play on, making the park a bright and playful place for everyone in the neighborhood to visit.

pages.text: People decorated this pocket park with many lights. They twinkle at night.
pages.brief: Show a pocket park at night, decorated with many lights that twinkle around the park; people have decorated this pocket park with the many lights, so the park looks bright in the dark city night.

pages.text: An artist made a statue for this pocket park. It reminds people of someone important.
pages.brief: Show an artist beside a statue standing in a pocket park inside the city; the artist made the statue for this park, and the statue reminds people of someone important as they look at it.

pages.text: This pocket park has grass and a large pond. People can come here to think.
pages.brief: Show a pocket park in the city with grass and a large pond; show people coming to this park to sit quietly and think beside the water, where it is calm and peaceful for them.

pages.text: A man paints a big snake and turtle in this pocket park. They look as if they would be fun to play on.
pages.brief: Show a man painting a big snake and a big turtle in a pocket park; the painted animals look as if they would be fun for people to play on as the man paints them.

pages.text: This tiny pocket park is almost hidden in trees. People can relax and listen to the waterfall.
pages.brief: Show a tiny pocket park in the city, almost hidden among trees, with a waterfall inside it, and show people quietly relaxing there in the park as they listen to the sound of the waterfall.

pages.text: Conclusion Pocket parks can be found all over. Do you have a pocket park where you live?
pages.brief: Show pocket parks in many different places all over a city, and show a person looking around a neighborhood as if wondering whether there is a pocket park somewhere near where they live in the city.

books.title: The Butterfly Life Cycle
books.art_why: Monarch butterflies and their life stages exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: The Butterfly Life Cycle.
pages.brief: A monarch butterfly with orange and black wings rests on a green leaf in a sunny garden, wings spread open. Soft light falls on the butterfly and leaf. The butterfly's body is slim and dark, and its antennae curve forward.

pages.text: The Life Cycle A monarch butterfly has four stages in its life cycle.
pages.brief: A monarch butterfly with bright orange and black wings rests on a green leaf in a sunny meadow. Its wings are fully open, and its thin antennae point forward. Sunlight shines around it. The butterfly's body is dark and slender.

pages.text: Egg A female monarch butterfly lays an egg on a leaf. A caterpillar grows inside the tiny egg. The egg hatches in three to twelve days.
pages.brief: A female monarch butterfly, orange and black, rests on a broad green leaf and lays a tiny pale egg on the leaf. A small caterpillar grows inside the egg. Sunlight falls on the leaf. The egg sits near the leaf edge.

pages.text: The hungry caterpillar eats all the time. First, the caterpillar eats its own eggshell. Then, the caterpillar eats the leaf it is on.
pages.brief: A small monarch caterpillar, striped black, yellow and white, clings to a green leaf and chews its edge. Beside it, a broken eggshell rests on the leaf. The caterpillar crawls forward, eating. Its mouth is at the leaf edge.

pages.text: The caterpillar grows quickly. Its skin does not grow. The caterpillar’s skin splits and peels away.
pages.brief: A monarch caterpillar clings to a green leaf as its old skin splits and peels away from its body. New skin shows underneath. The caterpillar is striped black, yellow and white, and it looks larger.

pages.text: Do You Know? Monarch caterpillars only eat the leaves of the milkweed plant. New skin is under the old skin. The caterpillar sheds its skin four to six times. The caterpillar grows for two to four weeks.
pages.brief: A black, yellow and white striped monarch caterpillar clings to a broad milkweed leaf and chews its edge. A thin piece of old skin peels back along its body, showing new skin beneath. More milkweed leaves surround it.

pages.text: Pupa When the caterpillar is grown, it hangs from a branch. It sheds its skin one last time. The new skin is bright green.
pages.brief: A full-grown monarch caterpillar hangs upside down from a thin branch. Its old skin splits and peels away one last time. The new skin underneath is bright green. Green leaves surround the branch. The caterpillar's striped body shows.

pages.text: This green skin becomes hard. The caterpillar is now a pupa. It will stay inside its shell for one to two weeks.
pages.brief: A bright green pupa hangs from a thin branch, its surface hard and smooth. The green shell is closed around the changing caterpillar inside. Green leaves surround it in soft light. The pupa hangs upside down.

pages.text: Adult Butterfly The pupa comes out of its shell. It is now a butterfly. Its wings are wet.
pages.brief: A monarch butterfly comes out of a split green pupa shell, hanging from a branch. Its orange and black wings are crumpled and wet. Pieces of the shell stay nearby. The new butterfly rests beside the empty shell.

pages.text: The new butterfly rests. The butterfly must hang upside down, or it will not be able to fly.
pages.brief: A newly emerged monarch butterfly hangs upside down from a thin branch. Its orange and black wings are still wet and folded. The butterfly rests quietly, holding its upside-down position. Green leaves blur behind it.

pages.text: The butterfly hangs for three to four hours. The sun and air dry its wings.
pages.brief: The monarch butterfly hangs upside down from a branch in warm sunlight. Its orange and black wings spread slightly as the sun and air dry them. A soft breeze moves the leaves around it. The butterfly stays still.

pages.text: Then, the butterfly is able to fly. It flies off to eat. It also searches for a mate.
pages.brief: The monarch butterfly flies away from the branch, wings open, over green plants. It flies toward bright flowers to eat. Another monarch butterfly flies nearby, and the two search for a mate. Sunlight fills the meadow.

pages.text: A monarch butterfly may only live for two to six weeks. The female monarch lays her eggs. The butterfly life cycle starts again.
pages.brief: A female monarch butterfly rests on a green leaf and lays a tiny egg on the leaf. An adult monarch butterfly flies nearby. Sunlight falls on the leaf, and the egg waits. The cycle begins again with this egg.

books.title: Elephants: Giant Mammals
books.art_why: Elephants and their habitats exist in the real world today, so real photographs fit best.

pages.text: Elephants are Number One! Elephants are huge! They are much, much bigger than the biggest human. They are the biggest land animals on Earth.
pages.brief: A wide outdoor view of enormous elephants standing on open grassland, their bodies towering high. Beside them, a full-grown human stands far below the elephants' height, showing just how much bigger these animals are than the biggest person.

pages.text: Take a Look Elephants are covered with thick gray or brown skin. They have long noses called trunks.
pages.brief: A close view of an elephant's body and head outdoors, showing thick gray or brown wrinkled skin. Its long nose, the trunk, hangs down in front, clearly visible from base to tip against the natural background.

pages.text: Elephants use their trunks to breathe and make noise. They also use their trunks to grab food and suck up water.
pages.brief: An elephant stands outdoors using its trunk. The trunk is lifted to breathe and make noise, then reaches out to grasp food, and finally dips down to suck up water from a pool, all shown in one clear natural scene.

pages.text: Two Kinds of Elephants There are African and Asian elephants. African elephants are bigger than Asian elephants. The two kinds are different in other ways, too.
pages.brief: Two elephants stand side by side outdoors for comparison. The African elephant is clearly larger, while the Asian elephant beside it is smaller. Both are shown in full view so their different sizes and appearances can be seen.

pages.text: Baby elephants weigh more than most adult humans. The mother teaches her calf how to live in the wild.
pages.brief: A mother elephant stands close to her calf out in the wild. The calf is already large and heavy. The mother stays near, guiding and teaching her young one how to live in its natural surroundings.

pages.text: Elephants live in groups like a family. Adult elephants in the group help keep the young ones safe.
pages.brief: A family group of elephants stands together outdoors on open ground. Several adult elephants surround the smaller young ones, staying close beside them and keeping the calves safe within the group.

pages.text: Don’t Eat Me! Huge elephants don’t have to worry about other animals. Lions and tigers know adult elephants are too big to attack.
pages.brief: Adult elephants stand peacefully on the grassland. Nearby, lions and tigers watch from a distance but keep back, not attacking, because the adult elephants are far too big and powerful to take on.

pages.text: Time to Leave After ten to fifteen years, young males leave their groups. They go to live alone or with other males. Female elephants stay together in their own group.
pages.brief: A young male elephant walks away from his family group across open ground, heading off alone. Behind him, the female elephants remain together, standing close in their own group on the landscape.

pages.text: Plenty of Plants Elephants eat a lot of grass and leaves in one day. It takes an adult human one hundred days to eat as much.
pages.brief: Elephants stand among plenty of plants, pulling up grass and stripping leaves to eat. A large pile of greenery shows how much they consume in a day, far more than a human would eat.

pages.text: Asian and African Giants Elephants are smart animals that take good care of each other. They are very special animals.
pages.brief: Asian and African elephants stand together outdoors as giant animals. Adults and young stay close, caring for one another, showing how smart and special these huge mammals are in their natural world.

books.title: Condors: Giant Birds
books.art_why: Condors are real animals that exist today, so photographs can show them.

pages.text: A Very Big Bird Condors are huge birds. One wing can be almost as long as a bicycle.
pages.brief: A huge condor is shown as a very big bird, with one long wing stretched out near a bicycle. The wing reaches almost the length of the bicycle, making clear just how large this bird is.

pages.text: Condor Homes These big birds like wide-open spaces. They need lots of room to land.
pages.brief: These big condors are in wide-open spaces where they have lots of room. The birds need that open space to land, so they are seen in a broad, open setting with plenty of room around them.

pages.text: Condors fly high to look for food. They can fly for a long time.
pages.brief: Condors fly high in the sky above as they look for food. They can stay flying for a long time, so the scene shows the large birds soaring high while searching for something to eat.

pages.text: Condors live in high places. They dry their wings in the sun after bathing. They make nests on rocky cliffs and in trees.
pages.brief: Condors live in high places. They dry their wings in the sun after bathing, and they make nests on rocky cliffs and in trees. The scene shows condors in high places, with their wings spread to dry in the sunlight.

pages.text: Time to Clean Up Condors can eat all kinds of dead animals. They may eat a small rabbit or a big whale.
pages.brief: Condors eat all kinds of dead animals. One condor may eat a small rabbit, while another may eat a big whale. The scene shows condors cleaning up by feeding on these dead animals, from a small rabbit to a big whale.

pages.text: Condors can eat dead animals without getting sick.
pages.brief: Condors can eat dead animals without getting sick. A condor is shown with a dead animal as food, and it remains healthy after eating. The scene focuses on the condor eating dead animals and staying well, without becoming sick.

pages.text: What Makes a Condor a Bird? All birds • have a backbone • have feathers • have wings.
pages.brief: All birds have a backbone, feathers, and wings. A condor is shown as a bird with a backbone, feathers, and wings. The scene focuses on these three parts that make a condor a bird clearly.

pages.text: From the Neck Up Some condors have white feathers around their necks. Others are all black. Condors do not have feathers on their heads.
pages.brief: Some condors have white feathers around their necks, while others are all black. Condors do not have feathers on their heads. The scene shows condors from the neck up, with white neck feathers on some and all-black bodies on others.

pages.text: Condor heads can change colors. The color shows how the condors are feeling.
pages.brief: Condor heads can change colors. The color shows how the condors are feeling. The scene shows a condor's head in different colors, with each color showing a different feeling. The head changes from one color to another.

pages.text: Condors Grow Up Mother condors lay one egg every two years. Both parents take care of the egg. The baby condor comes out of the egg after two months. Six months later, it starts to fly. Condors can live almost as long as a person.
pages.brief: A mother condor lays one egg every two years, and both parents take care of the egg. The baby condor comes out after two months, and six months later it starts to fly. Condors can live almost as long as a person.

pages.text: There are very few condors today. People watch condors to keep them safe.
pages.brief: There are very few condors today. People watch condors to keep them safe. The scene shows people in the present day watching the few condors close by, staying with them to help keep them safe.

pages.text: Big Wings in the Sky Condors are special birds. They are some of the largest flying birds in the world.
pages.brief: Condors are special birds. They are some of the largest flying birds in the world. The scene shows condors with big wings in the sky, as special birds that are among the largest flying birds in the world.

books.title: Blue Whales: Giant Mammals
books.art_why: Blue whales are real animals that can be photographed in the ocean today.

pages.text: A Whale of an Animal The blue whale is the biggest animal on Earth. It is longer than three school buses. It is as heavy as thirty-three elephants!
pages.brief: A single blue whale fills the open ocean, its long, enormous body stretching through blue water. The whale is seen from the side, mouth closed, flippers out, surface light above. Its immense size is clear against the empty water around it.

pages.text: All mammals Look Out for the Spout A blue whale has two holes on top of its head. The whale uses the holes to breathe.
pages.brief: Close-up view of the top of a blue whale's head at the ocean surface. Two blowholes sit side by side on the crown. The whale's dark, smooth skin is visible, and calm water surrounds the head as the whale breathes.

pages.text: The blue whale swims to the surface of the ocean. Water and air shoot up from the holes!
pages.brief: The blue whale rises to the surface of the ocean. A tall spout of water and air shoots up from the two holes on its head. The whale's back and head break the surface, with open water all around.

pages.text: Listen for the Song Blue whales sing as they swim. Whale songs are low and loud. The song can be heard far away.
pages.brief: Two blue whales swim together in deep blue water. Their long bodies glide side by side, mouths closed. The low, loud song travels through the ocean around them, far beyond the whales in the wide, dim water.

pages.text: Filling Up on Small Stuff Blue whales eat tiny animals and plants. Blue whales dive to find food.
pages.brief: A blue whale dives down through the ocean toward a drifting cloud of tiny animals and plants. The whale's huge body angles downward, mouth closed, while the small food spreads through the dark blue water ahead.

pages.text: A whale opens its mouth. Tiny animals and plants flow in with the water.
pages.brief: An open blue whale mouth fills the frame underwater. Water rushes in, carrying a swirl of tiny animals and plants. The whale's enormous lower jaw is stretched wide, and the small food flows toward the dark opening.

pages.text: A blue whale has baleen in its mouth. Baleen is like stiff hair.
pages.brief: Inside a blue whale's open mouth, rows of baleen hang down like stiff hair. The pale, fringed plates line the upper jaw. The whale's mouth is partly open in the water, showing the baleen clearly against the dark inside.

pages.text: The water goes out through the baleen. The food stays inside.
pages.brief: A blue whale's mouth is shown with baleen in place. Water flows out through the stiff, hair-like plates while tiny animals and plants stay trapped inside. The whale's huge jaw and the fringed baleen fill the underwater view.

pages.text: Blue whales eat a lot. The food helps them grow blubber. Blubber is a kind of fat. It keeps the whales warm in cold water.
pages.brief: A blue whale swims through cold, deep blue water. Its body is thick and rounded, with a smooth, heavy shape. Tiny food drifts nearby, and the whale's great bulk is clear as it moves through the chilly ocean.

pages.text: Great Big Babies A calf drinks a lot of milk each day. It grows larger every hour.
pages.brief: A blue whale mother floats in the ocean beside her calf. The calf is close to her underside, drinking milk. The young whale looks small next to its mother but sturdy, growing larger as it feeds in the calm water.

pages.text: A blue whale mother has one calf at The calf stays with her for a year. Then it swims off to live on its own.
pages.brief: A blue whale mother swims in open ocean while her single calf moves a little apart, beginning to swim on its own. The mother's long body is behind the smaller calf; both are alone in the wide blue water.

pages.text: The Biggest Animals Blue whales are huge mammals. They are the biggest animals on Earth.
pages.brief: A huge blue whale swims through the wide ocean, its body filling the blue water. The whale is alone, mouth closed, flippers out, surface light above. Its enormous size shows it is among the biggest animals on Earth.

books.title: The Mighty Mississippi
books.art_why: A real river, boats, cities and wildlife can be photographed.

pages.text: The Mighty Mississippi.
pages.brief: A broad, powerful river winds across a green landscape beneath a wide sky in this opening scene, suggesting the mighty Mississippi before its long journey begins, with calm water stretching toward the far wide horizon.

pages.text: A Long Journey Rain falls. It mixes into the clear waters of a lake.
pages.brief: Rain falls steadily onto a clear lake, dimpling the calm surface as fresh drops mix into the water. The lake lies open and quiet beneath the rain, with clear water spreading outward before it begins to flow onward.

pages.text: The lake flows into a river. A child could wade across here. This is where the mighty Mississippi River begins.
pages.brief: The clear lake flows into a small, shallow river. A child wades across the gentle water, showing how low and narrow it is here. This calm, quiet spot is where the mighty Mississippi River begins.

pages.text: The water will travel through ten of the fifty United States. It will take three months to reach the sea.
pages.brief: The river’s water travels onward through a long stretch of varied land, passing green fields, wooded hills, and open plains. The scene suggests a journey through ten states and three months before the water finally reaches the sea.

pages.text: The Upper River At first, the river flows through many locks and dams. They raise or lower the water around the boats. This makes it safe for boats to travel. They also hold back water so boats don’t hit the river bottom.
pages.brief: On the upper river, locks and dams hold back the water and raise or lower boats around them. A boat waits inside a lock as the water level changes, keeping the vessel safe and away from the river bottom.

pages.text: Boats on this part of the river carry wheat and corn down south. The grain helps feed the world.
pages.brief: Boats on the upper river carry loads of wheat and corn down south. A wide barge moves slowly along the water, filled with golden grain, ready to help feed many people far beyond the riverbanks.

pages.text: A big, dirty river comes in from the west. It mixes with the clear waters of the Mississippi. The Mississippi grows wide and brown.
pages.brief: A big, dirty river comes in from the west and mixes with the clear Mississippi. The two waters meet and blend, and the Mississippi grows wide and brown as the muddy river spreads slowly into it.

pages.text: The Lower River Another big river comes in from the east. It joins the Mississippi, too. The river grows deep and even wider.
pages.brief: Another big river comes in from the east and joins the Mississippi. The two rivers merge in a broad stretch of water, making the Mississippi grow deep and even wider as the combined current flows onward.

pages.text: The Mississippi often floods. The floods are messy, but they leave behind rich soil.
pages.brief: The Mississippi overflows its banks, spreading messy, muddy floodwater across fields and low land. When the floodwater finally pulls back slowly, it leaves behind rich, dark soil on the ground, ready to help new plants grow.

pages.text: The lower part of the river has big cities, too.
pages.brief: Along the lower part of the river, big cities rise beside the water. Many tall buildings stand near the wide Mississippi, showing that people live and work in this busy, crowded lower stretch of the river.

pages.text: Boats carry iron, steel, rubber, paper, and wood. Some of these things move back up the river. Some move farther south.
pages.brief: Boats carry iron, steel, rubber, paper, and wood along the long busy river. Barges loaded with heavy metal coils, paper rolls, rubber, and lumber move some goods back up the river and some farther south.

pages.text: Bald eagles nest in tall trees along the upper river. Alligators swim in the lower river, where the water is warmer. River otters play in the upper river. Pallid sturgeon enter with the Missouri River.
pages.brief: Bald eagles nest in tall trees along the upper river, while river otters play nearby. In the warmer lower river, alligators swim through the water. Pallid sturgeon enter where the Missouri River joins, adding another kind of fish to the river.

pages.text: The Mighty Mississippi The rain that fell on the lake has reached the sea at last. Some of that water may return to the lake as rain some day. It may make the journey all over again.
pages.brief: The water that fell as rain on the lake has reached the sea at last. Far away, clouds gather over the lake again, hinting that some of that water may return as rain and make the journey all over again.

books.title: What Built This?
books.art_why: Real animals and their structures exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Animal Builders Not all builders are human. Some builders are animals! What do they build?
pages.brief: A group of different animals are shown in natural settings, each busy making or tending a structure. Some gather natural materials while others arrange what they have made. The scene presents animal builders at work and invites wondering what each one is building.

pages.text: Prairie Dog Towns These animals dig underground tunnels. They make rooms for eating and sleeping.
pages.brief: Prairie dogs dig underground tunnels. Inside their tunnel system, they make rooms for eating and sleeping. Show the animals at work in the soil, with tunnels branching out and separate rooms where they eat or rest.

pages.text: Sociable Weaver Bird Nests These birds make nests from sticks and grass. One nest holds hundreds of birds!
pages.brief: Many sociable weaver birds gather around a large nest made from sticks and grass. One nest holds hundreds of birds. Show the birds perched on and near the woven nest, adding sticks and grass to the shared structure.

pages.text: Termite Mounds These little insects chew wood. They build huge piles with the wood and mud.
pages.brief: Small termites chew pieces of wood. They build huge mounds using the wood and mud. Show the insects at work near a tall termite mound, with bits of wood and mud making up the structure around them.

pages.text: Pufferfish Circles This male fish makes sand art on the floor of the sea. A female fish lays her eggs there.
pages.brief: A male pufferfish makes a circular sand design on the sea floor. A female pufferfish lays her eggs in the sand art. Show the fish and the circled pattern underwater, with the eggs resting in the sand.

pages.text: Spider Trapdoors This spider digs a tunnel. It makes a door with its silk. The spider opens the door and prey falls through.
pages.brief: A spider digs a tunnel and makes a door with its silk. The spider opens the door, and prey falls through. Show the spider at the tunnel entrance in a natural setting, with the silk door and the prey.

pages.text: Underground Ant City Millions of ants build underground cities with tunnels that go all over.
pages.brief: Millions of ants build an underground city. Their tunnels spread out in every direction through the soil. Show great numbers of ants moving through the many connected tunnels of the underground city, deep in the soil.

pages.text: Little Ants, Big City People found this huge underground city in South America. It is empty now, but it used to be the home of leafcutter ants. They had to work hard and move a lot of soil to make a home this big!
pages.brief: A huge underground city in South America is shown empty now. It used to be home to leafcutter ants. They worked hard and moved a lot of soil to make this big home. Show the vast tunnels and chambers.

pages.text: Paper Wasp Nests These insects chew bits of wood and plants into paper. They make an amazing nest.
pages.brief: Paper wasps chew bits of wood and plants into a paper-like material. They use it to make an amazing nest. Show the insects at work on the nest, with bits of wood and plant material nearby.

pages.text: Crayfish Chimneys This animal digs into wet dirt to get to water. The dirt gets pushed up and looks.
pages.brief: A crayfish digs down into wet dirt to reach water. The dirt it pushes up rises around the opening and looks like a small chimney. Show the crayfish at the muddy opening with the pushed-up dirt mound.

pages.text: Beaver Dams and Dens Beavers use sticks and mud to build dams and dens. Dens are underwater, so beavers have to swim into them. The living space is built above the water level so that it stays dry.
pages.brief: Beavers use sticks and mud to build dams and dens. The den entrance is underwater, so beavers swim into it, while the living space stays above the water level and dry. Show beavers at the dam and den.

pages.text: Caddisfly Cocoons These little insects use their silk to make cocoons. They add sand, small sticks, and even shells. They make their homes look like pieces of art. Watch Them Build Animals don’t need tools to build great things. Animals are amazing!
pages.brief: Little caddisfly insects use silk to make cocoons. They add sand, small sticks, and even shells. Their homes look like pieces of art. Show the decorated cocoons close up in a clear view covered with these natural bits.

books.title: Earth's Water
books.art_why: Water in ponds, oceans, ice and weather is real and photographed today.

pages.text: Earth’s Water.
pages.brief: Planet Earth seen from space, a round blue globe with swirling white clouds and dark ocean water covering most of its surface, alone against the black of space, filling the middle of the picture.

pages.text: Water Everywhere Water is in ponds, lakes, and oceans. It flows in rivers and streams. It is in the air and frozen as snow and ice.
pages.brief: A wide natural view showing water in many places at once: a still pond, a big lake, the ocean, a river and a narrow stream running between stones, with snow and ice on a cold hillside above and open air over it all.

pages.text: Most of Earth is covered with water. Plants and animals need water to live. Earth’s Water.
pages.brief: Earth photographed from space, its surface mostly blue water with white cloud swirls. Below, a green leafy plant grows and a small animal stands beside a pond, both close to the water they need.

pages.text: What are some ways you use Earth’s water?
pages.brief: Water being used at home: a kitchen tap running into a glass, a garden sprinkler spraying over green grass, and a bathtub filling with water, showing everyday ways people use water in their houses and gardens.

pages.text: Different Forms of Water Most of the water we see is a liquid. Liquid water takes the shape of the container it is in. Earth’s Water.
pages.brief: Liquid water poured into three different containers on a table: a tall glass, a round jug and a wide bowl. The water has taken the shape of each container, flat on top and clear.

pages.text: Not all water is liquid. When water gets very cold, it freezes. It becomes solid. Solid water is called ice.
pages.brief: A freezer tray of ice cubes and a solid block of ice on a cold surface, frosty and hard, showing water that has frozen solid after getting very cold.

pages.text: Much of Earth’s frozen water is at the North and South Poles. Earth’s Water.
pages.brief: The North and South Poles: a vast white ice sheet stretching to the horizon, cracked glaciers and tall icebergs floating in dark polar water under a pale, freezing sky.

pages.text: Some of Earth’s water is invisible. It is in the air. This water is a gas.
pages.brief: A wide view of a lake under open sky, the air above the water soft and hazy. The water in the air is a gas and cannot be seen, only the shimmering air above the lake.

pages.text: Changing Water Water is always changing. When frozen water is heated, it melts. It changes to a liquid. When liquid water gets cold, it freezes. It changes to ice. Earth’s Water.
pages.brief: Two changes side by side: an ice cube melting into a small pool of liquid water on a warm surface, and a tray of water turning to solid ice in a cold place, frost spreading across it.

pages.text: Have you ever seen a puddle of water dry up on a hot day? Energy from the Sun changed the liquid water into a gas. This is called evaporation.
pages.brief: A small puddle on warm pavement shrinking under a bright hot sun in a clear sky, its edges drying inward, leaving a faint damp patch on the grey stone.

pages.text: When invisible water in the air gets cold, it can make clouds. Clouds are tiny drops of liquid water. Those drops can get bigger. Then they fall as rain. Earth’s Water.
pages.brief: White clouds building in the sky above a landscape, made of tiny water drops, growing heavier and darker until drops of rain fall in streaks onto the ground below.

pages.text: Water Is Important Rain keeps plants alive. We fight fires with water. Animals take baths in water.
pages.brief: Three scenes of water at work: rain falling on green plants in a garden, firefighters spraying a strong jet of water onto a burning building, and animals splashing and washing themselves in a river.

pages.text: It is important to take care of Earth’s water. Polluted water makes people, plants, and animals sick. Would you want to drink and play in polluted water? Earth’s Water.
pages.brief: A stream running dull and dirty, litter and waste floating in the brown water. A plant on the bank droops and wilts beside the polluted water, which nobody should drink or play in.

books.title: Nature Stinks!
books.art_why: Real animals and plants alive today, shown with real photographs.

pages.text: Stinky Nature Some animals smell bad. Some plants smell bad, too. Being stinky helps some plants and animals stay alive.
pages.brief: A wide nature scene with several animals and plants that smell bad: a furry animal, a bird, a bug, a turtle, a frog and a big flower. They stand among leaves and grass, showing that being stinky helps them stay alive.

pages.text: Stinky Furry Animals This animal sprays a stinky liquid when enemies get close.
pages.brief: A furry animal stands in grass, facing enemies that come close. It sprays a cloud of stinky liquid from its body toward them, and the enemies pull back from the smell.

pages.text: This animal plays dead if enemies get close. It also makes stinky green slime.
pages.brief: A furry animal lies still on the ground with its eyes closed, playing dead while an enemy stands nearby. A pool of stinky green slime spreads from its body across the ground, and the enemy backs away.

pages.text: A Very Stinky Plant The corpse flower stinks! A corpse is a dead body, and this plant smells like one. The plant’s bad smell brings flies and beetles near. This animal shoots a stinky liquid at its enemies.
pages.brief: A huge corpse flower opens wide in the rainforest, its bad smell drawing flies and beetles to land on it. Nearby, a small animal shoots a stream of stinky liquid at enemies that come too close, and the enemies retreat.

pages.text: This animal makes stinky liquid to keep other animals away. It also pees on food it doesn’t eat right away. The smell may keep other animals away.
pages.brief: An animal stands beside a pile of food it has not eaten. It makes a stinky liquid and pees on the food, and the bad smell keeps other animals away. The other animals turn and move off.

pages.text: This animal fights over mates. It uses stinky pee to keep others away.
pages.brief: Two animals fight over mates in an open space, pushing and facing each other. Around them, stinky pee marks the ground, and the smell keeps other animals away from the pair.

pages.text: Stinky Birds This bird eats leaves. Tiny living things in its body break down the leaves. This way of eating makes it smell bad.
pages.brief: A bird perches on a branch and eats leaves. Inside its body, tiny living things are shown breaking the leaves down, and a bad smell rises from the bird as it feeds.

pages.text: This bird eats dead animals. It throws up when enemies get close! Its throw-up smells very bad.
pages.brief: A bird stands over a dead animal and eats it. When an enemy comes close, the bird throws up toward the enemy, and the smelly throw-up lands on the ground between them. The enemy turns away.

pages.text: Stinky Bugs This bug sprays a hot, stinky liquid when enemies get close. The liquid is so hot that it can kill some enemies.
pages.brief: A bug faces enemies that come close. It sprays a hot, stinky liquid from its body, and the liquid hits the enemies. The spray is so hot that some enemies fall dead.

pages.text: This bug is too slow to run away. It makes a stinky liquid when enemies get close.
pages.brief: A slow bug crawls along the ground, too slow to run away from enemies. When enemies come close, it makes a stinky liquid that spreads around it and keeps them back.

pages.text: Other Stinky Animals This turtle is also called “stinkpot”! It smells bad when enemies get close. This frog smells like rotten onions when enemies get close.
pages.brief: A turtle sits in shallow water, smelling bad as enemies come close. Nearby, a frog crouches on a leaf and gives off the smell of rotten onions. Both animals stay still as the smell keeps enemies away.

pages.text: Good and Stinky Some animals smell bad. Some plants smell bad, too. Being stinky helps some plants and animals stay alive.
pages.brief: A wide scene brings together smelly animals and plants: a furry animal, a bird, a bug, a turtle, a frog and a big flower. Each one gives off a bad smell that helps it stay alive among the leaves and grass.

books.title: Yellowstone: A Place of Wild Wonders
books.art_why: The keyword check points to drawing, and the book includes ancient hot-spot and Native history along with landscape scenes.

pages.text: Yellowstone: A Place of Wild Wonders.
pages.brief: A broad, welcoming view of Yellowstone's natural landscape under an open sky, introducing a place of wild wonders. Keep the scene simple, with land and sky, and no extra people, events, or objects beyond the landscape.

pages.text: Introduction National parks are areas of protected land. In 1872, Yellowstone became the first national park. What can people see there?
pages.brief: A wide protected landscape of Yellowstone, with open land and natural features, presented as the first national park from 1872. A few visitors stand at a distance, looking at what people can see there in a calm natural setting.

pages.text: A Hot Spot People go to Yellowstone to see Old Faithful. Old Faithful is one of the geysers. It shoots steam and hot water high into the air. Yellowstone Supervolcano Yellowstone is home to an old caved-in volcano. The volcano is very big. It doesn’t look as if it is going to erupt again soon.
pages.brief: A scene in Yellowstone where Old Faithful geyser shoots steam and hot water high into the air. Nearby show the very big, old caved-in volcano that makes up the Yellowstone Supervolcano, calm and not appearing about to erupt soon.

pages.text: Yellowstone is on top of a hot spot. The hot spot made geysers, hot springs, and hot mud pools.
pages.brief: A scene in Yellowstone where the ground sits on top of a hot spot. The hot spot has made geysers, hot springs, and hot mud pools. Show these steaming natural features in the park, with hot water and bubbling mud under an open sky.

pages.text: Wildlife More than 350 kinds of animals live in Yellowstone.
pages.brief: More than 350 kinds of animals live in Yellowstone. Show a varied wildlife scene in the park, with many different animals spread across the land, some standing, some moving, and some resting, all living in Yellowstone's natural setting.

pages.text: These animals are big and hairy. They roll on the ground to get rid of flies.
pages.brief: Big, hairy animals roll on the ground in Yellowstone to get rid of flies. Show several of these large, shaggy animals lying and rolling in the dust, with flies nearby, in an open grassy area inside the park.

pages.text: These animals are big but fast. They sleep in dens all winter.
pages.brief: Big but fast animals sleep in dens all winter in Yellowstone. Show these large, quick animals curled up asleep inside winter dens, with snow and bare trees outside in the cold park landscape around them.

pages.text: These animals were forced out of Yellowstone. People brought them back later.
pages.brief: Animals that were forced out of Yellowstone are shown returning, after people brought them back later. Show these animals moving quietly through the park again, with people at a distance in an open natural setting.

pages.text: History Native peoples lived in Yellowstone before it was a national park.
pages.brief: Native peoples lived in Yellowstone before it was a national park. Show Native people in the Yellowstone landscape, living and moving through the land in a natural setting, with no modern park buildings around them.

pages.text: More people went to Yellowstone and knew it had to be protected.
pages.brief: More people went to Yellowstone and knew it had to be protected. Show a group of visitors standing in the park, looking at its natural wonders, while the land around them is cared for and kept safe.

pages.text: Today, there are many more national parks.
pages.brief: Today, there are many more national parks. Show several large protected natural landscapes side by side, each with its own land, water, and sky, stretching across a wide view to suggest the many national parks today.

pages.text: Conclusion Many people go to Yellowstone every year. They go to fish, hike, and camp in the park.
pages.brief: Many people go to Yellowstone every year. Show visitors fishing, hiking, and camping in the park, with fishing gear, walking paths, tents, and campfire scenes spread through a wide natural Yellowstone setting under an open sky.

pages.text: All national parks are great places to see. Yellowstone was the first!
pages.brief: All national parks are great places to see, and Yellowstone was the first. Show a grand view of Yellowstone's natural wonders, with geysers and wildlife, and other national park landscapes beyond, presenting them as great places to see.

books.title: The Grand Canyon
books.art_why: The book includes the 1869 journey and Native history, where real photos of those moments are not possible.

pages.text: The Grand Canyon.
pages.brief: A sweeping view of the Grand Canyon’s tall, layered rock walls and a deep valley under a bright sky. The huge landscape stretches wide, with no people or animals visible, showing the grand scale of the place.

pages.text: Grand Grand THE CANYON CANYON CANYON.
pages.brief: A wide, open view of the Grand Canyon’s rocky walls and deep valley, with layered stone stretching across the scene under a clear sky. The landscape is quiet and grand, with no people or animals in sight.

pages.text: A Canyon So Grand The Grand Canyon is so big that it can be seen from space. It became a national park in 1919.
pages.brief: A view from space shows Earth with the Grand Canyon visible as a long, winding shape across the land. The canyon looks enormous from high above, stretching across the landscape. Its huge size is clear even from far away.

pages.text: A national park is an area of protected land. Incredible Condors Look up! Giant birds called California condors live in the Grand Canyon. They almost died out. People caught them and kept them safe so they could have babies.
pages.brief: California condors with huge wings soar above the Grand Canyon’s rocky walls. Below, people carefully care for young condors in a protected place, helping the giant birds stay safe so they can have babies. The birds are rare and special.

pages.text: Formation The Colorado River made the Grand Canyon through erosion. Erosion happens when some of the ground is worn away. The river ran over the earth, and after many years, a canyon was made.
pages.brief: The Colorado River flows through the Grand Canyon, wearing away rock and soil over time. The moving water cuts into the earth, showing how erosion slowly carves a deep canyon. Small pieces of ground are carried away by the river.

pages.text: The Grand Canyon is striped with colors. The stripes are layers of sediment that built up on top of each other. They show how Earth has changed over time.
pages.brief: The Grand Canyon’s rock walls show colorful stripes, with one layer of sediment on top of another. These layers built up over time and reveal how the Earth has changed. The bands of color run across the canyon sides.

pages.text: Home in the Grand Canyon The Havasupai (hah-vuh-SOO-py), Navajo (NAH-vuh-hoh), Hualapai (WAH-luh-py), Hopi (HOH-pee), Zuni (ZOO-nee), and Apache (uh-PA-chee) tribes live in the Grand Canyon. Their lives are different from their relatives’ from long ago. But they have passed down many stories and traditions. Exploration Native people lived in the Grand Canyon. Many still do today.
pages.brief: Native people from the Havasupai, Navajo, Hualapai, Hopi, Zuni, and Apache tribes live in the Grand Canyon area. Families share stories and traditions, and many Native people still make their homes there today. Their lives are different from long ago.

pages.text: In 1869, a group of Americans went to the canyon. Native people helped them learn about it.
pages.brief: In 1869, a group of Americans travels to the Grand Canyon with Native people who help them learn about the place. The explorers and their guides stand near the rocky canyon, looking out at the landscape.

pages.text: The Grand Canyon became a national park. Today, Native people help protect it. A Tale of Two Rims The South Rim of the Grand Canyon is very popular. It is open every day of the year. Across the canyon is the North Rim. The North Rim is much higher up, so it gets more snow. It is only open for the warmer months of the year.
pages.brief: The South Rim of the Grand Canyon is busy and open all year. Across the canyon, the higher North Rim has more snow and is open only in warmer months. Native people help protect the park today.

pages.text: Make Your Own Adventure Many people go to the Grand Canyon every year.
pages.brief: Many people visit the Grand Canyon every year. They stand near the canyon edge and look out at the wide view, ready to make their own adventure. The scene is full of visitors enjoying the famous place.

pages.text: Some people hike to the bottom of the canyon. They can walk around the bottom of the canyon for weeks.
pages.brief: Some people hike down into the Grand Canyon, following a trail to the bottom. At the bottom, they can walk around for weeks, exploring the deep valley. The hikers move along the rocky path. They go deep below the rim.

pages.text: Some people raft on the Colorado River. The river is very long.
pages.brief: Some people raft on the Colorado River inside the Grand Canyon. The long river carries the rafts through the canyon, with rocky walls rising on both sides. The river stretches far into the distance. Rafters ride the moving water.

pages.text: Some people walk by the canyon rim. The view from the rim is amazing.
pages.brief: Some people walk along the canyon rim, looking out at the amazing view. The Grand Canyon opens up below them, with layered rock walls and a huge valley stretching far away. They stand close to the edge.

pages.text: A Natural Wonder The Grand Canyon will be protected for years to come. People who go there are in for a view like nothing else.
pages.brief: The Grand Canyon is a natural wonder that will be protected for years to come. Visitors look out at a view like nothing else, with wide sky and deep canyon. The huge place stretches out before them.

books.title: Hawaii Volcanoes National Park
books.art_why: Real volcanoes, lava tubes, wildlife, plants and visitors exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: A Volcano Wonderland Hawaii Volcanoes National Park is on an island in Hawaii. A national park is protected land.
pages.brief: A green island in Hawaii rises from blue ocean, with a broad volcano shape at its center. Protected land stretches across the island, showing the national park as a volcano wonderland under a bright sky.

pages.text: Volcanoes Form a Park A volcano begins with hot, melted rocks deep in the Earth. The rocks push up through the ground. Then the rocks cool. Over time, the rocks build up into volcanoes.
pages.brief: A close view of a volcano shows glowing hot melted rock pushing up through a crack in the ground. Darker cooled rock has built up around the opening, forming the cone of a volcano under an open sky.

pages.text: Two special volcanoes are in Hawaii Volcanoes National Park.
pages.brief: Two special volcanoes stand on the island in the national park. One volcano rises beside the other, with rocky slopes and green land around them, showing the two volcanoes that make this park special.

pages.text: One volcano in the park is very active. Leaping Lava In 1959, one volcano shot lava higher in the air than the Eiffel Tower!
pages.brief: A very active volcano sends a tall fountain of bright orange lava leaping high into the air. The lava shoots upward from the volcano's vent, reaching far above the surrounding land in a dramatic eruption.

pages.text: Another volcano in the park is very big.
pages.brief: Another volcano in the park is very big. A wide, massive volcano fills the view, with long gentle slopes stretching across the land. It stands as a huge landmark beside the other volcano in the park.

pages.text: An Amazing History Hawaii Volcanoes National Park is 520 square miles (1,347 sq km). People have come to see the volcanoes for a long time.
pages.brief: People stand at a viewpoint and look out over the volcano landscape of Hawaii Volcanoes National Park. The protected land stretches wide around them, showing the 520 square miles of park that visitors have come to see for a long time.

pages.text: The land became a national park.
pages.brief: The land of Hawaii Volcanoes National Park is shown as protected national park land. A volcano rises over the landscape, with rocky ground and green plants, marking the place that became a national park.

pages.text: There are volcanoes and lava tubes. Lava tubes are big tunnels under the ground. People can walk through them.
pages.brief: People walk through a lava tube, a big tunnel under the ground. The tunnel has rocky walls and a rough ceiling, and the visitors move through the dark passage beneath the volcano landscape above.

pages.text: Wildlife at the Volcanoes’ Edge Hundreds of animals are protected in the park.
pages.brief: Wild animals are shown at the volcano's edge, with rocky ground and volcanic slopes behind them. The animals are protected in the park, and they live near the volcano in this safe national park land.

pages.text: Hundreds of plants are protected in the park.
pages.brief: Many green plants grow on the volcanic slopes of the park. The plants cover the rocky ground, showing the hundreds of protected plants that live in Hawaii Volcanoes National Park beside the volcanoes.

pages.text: Enjoy—But Watch Your Step! People can hike or camp in the park.
pages.brief: People hike along a trail in the park, carrying backpacks. Nearby, campers set up a tent on the ground. The visitors enjoy the park, walking and camping among the volcanoes and rocky landscape.

pages.text: When the volcanoes are active, parts of the park close. Hawaii Volcanoes National Park is fun to visit.
pages.brief: An active volcano sends steam and smoke into the sky while visitors watch from a safe distance. Parts of the park are closed near the active volcano, and people still enjoy visiting Hawaii Volcanoes National Park.

books.title: I Collect That!
books.art_why: Real people, everyday objects and collections all exist today, so photographs suit every page.

pages.text: Introduction Do you own a few stuffed animals? Then you have a collection. A collection is a group of things that are alike.
pages.brief: A group of stuffed animals sits together on a shelf, several soft toys of different sizes leaning against each other and filling the shelf from end to end in a bright room, arranged as one set.

pages.text: People collect things that they like. Some people collect rocks. Other people collect cars.
pages.brief: One person kneels beside a tray of collected rocks, turning a stone in hand, while nearby another person stands beside a row of cars lined up for display, both looking at their gathered things with interest.

pages.text: Collecting Is Cool A collection can be big or small, such as fifty stamps or ten baseball cards. Some people meet with other people who collect the same things.
pages.brief: A table holds an open stamp album with stamps arranged in rows and a small stack of baseball cards beside it. Several collectors sit around the table, talking and comparing the things they collect.

pages.text: A collection can be hard work. Some people like to care for their collection. They keep count of their things. They keep them clean.
pages.brief: A person wipes dust from a collected object with a soft cloth, then points at each item along a shelf, counting them one by one. Neat rows of objects fill the shelves behind, all clean and orderly.

pages.text: Common Collections Many people like to collect things that are easy to find. People collect coins and dolls. Math Minute Emma has 34 bookmarks in her collection. She gets 11 more for her birthday. How many bookmarks does she have now?
pages.brief: On a table, coins are sorted into small piles beside a row of dolls standing upright. Nearby, a girl holds a fan of bookmarks and counts them, her collection spread out in front of her.

pages.text: Some people collect things from places they visit.
pages.brief: A person places a small keepsake into a box filled with objects gathered from different places, each one different. A shelf behind holds more of these collected things, and the person pauses to look at the newest addition.

pages.text: Other people collect things they find outside.
pages.brief: Outdoors, a person walks along a path and bends to pick up a small object from the ground, adding it to a container held in one hand. More found objects sit in the container, gathered during time spent outside.

pages.text: You can also make art out of a collection.
pages.brief: A collection of small objects is arranged into a picture on a table, forming a shape or scene. A person steps back to look at the finished arrangement, which is made entirely from the gathered things, turning the collection into art.
