pages.text: You Collect What? Some people collect things based on type. It can take a long time to build a collection. One woman has more than eighteen thousand things with owls. She has owl shirts, owl toys, and more.
pages.brief: A woman wearing an owl shirt stands in a room full of owl things: owl toys on shelves, owl figures on tables, and owl items covering the walls. She holds one owl toy and smiles, surrounded by her enormous collection.

pages.text: One man has more than seven hundred locks. Wowser!
pages.brief: A man stands beside shelves and boxes filled with locks of many shapes and sizes. He holds one lock in his hand and looks at the rows of locks around him, a collection of more than seven hundred.

pages.text: Start Your Own Collection You can start a collection, too! Why not start with something easy, like fruit stickers? One woman has more than ten thousand!
pages.brief: A woman sits at a table with pages of fruit stickers spread out, peeling one sticker from its backing and placing it into a book. Rows of small, colorful fruit stickers fill the pages around her, part of a very large collection.

pages.text: A collection can also be really strange. Some people collect lists that other people have left behind in food stores! What would you like to collect?
pages.brief: A person stands near a food store holding a thick bundle of small papers gathered from the store, looking at them. Beside them, more of these collected papers are stacked, an unusual collection of things other people left behind.

books.title: Flies
books.art_why: Flies exist today and can be shown in real photographs.

pages.text: What Are Flies? Flies are insects. There are many kinds of flies.
pages.brief: Several different kinds of flies are shown together on a broad green leaf, each one a little different in size and colour, with clear wings and rounded bodies. They rest in warm daylight, showing that flies are insects and that many kinds of flies exist.

pages.text: Fly Bodies Flies have one pair of wings. They also have tiny arms that help them steer when they fly.
pages.brief: A single fly is shown in mid-flight, with one pair of clear wings beating and two tiny steering arms held out from its body. The small arms are visible near the wings, helping the fly change direction as it moves through the air.

pages.text: Flies have eyes that let them see all around. Each eye is made up of many little eyes.
pages.brief: A close view of a fly's head shows its large eyes wrapping around the sides, so it can see all around. Each big eye is made of many tiny little eyes packed closely together, covering the rounded surface of the head.

pages.text: How Flies Grow and Change All flies start as eggs. Each egg is tiny.
pages.brief: A fly is shown beside a cluster of very tiny eggs resting on a leaf or a patch of ground. The eggs are small and pale, and the adult fly stands nearby, showing that all flies begin life as eggs.

pages.text: Out of the egg comes a larva. The larva eats plants, fruits, or dead things. When the larva is grown, it forms a hard cover. It is now a pupa.
pages.brief: A larva is shown coming out of an egg, then eating a piece of fruit and a bit of dead plant material. Later the larva is shown inside a hard brown cover, formed around its body, now a pupa.

pages.text: The pupa changes inside the cover. When it comes out, it is an adult. Adult flies do not live very long. Their main job is to lay eggs to make more flies.
pages.brief: Inside a hard pupa cover, the fly is changing. The cover splits open and an adult fly comes out. The adult fly is shown standing near the empty case, then beside a small cluster of eggs, because its main job is to lay eggs.

pages.text: How Adult Flies Eat Adult flies drink all their food. They spit on solid food to turn it into goo. Then they drink the goo.
pages.brief: An adult fly is shown landing on a piece of solid food. It spits on the food, turning the spot into shiny goo, then lowers its mouth to drink the goo. The food and the fly's mouth are clearly shown.

pages.text: Flies and Germs Flies sometimes pick up germs from the things they eat. Some of the germs can make people sick.
pages.brief: A fly is shown walking over food scraps and rubbish, picking up tiny germs on its legs and body. The fly then stands near a person, and the germs are shown as tiny specks that can make people sick.

pages.text: Some flies suck blood. They can spread germs in the blood from one person to another.
pages.brief: A fly is shown biting through skin to suck blood. The same fly is shown later near another person, and tiny germs are shown moving from the fly's mouth into the skin, spreading germs from one person to another.

pages.text: Why Flies Are Important Flies spread pollen. Many plants need pollen to make seeds.
pages.brief: A fly is shown resting on a flower, with yellow pollen dust on its legs and body. The fly moves to another flower, carrying the pollen, and the plants are shown making seeds after the pollen is spread.

pages.text: Flies help break down dead plants and animals. Fly eggs and young are food for many other animals.
pages.brief: Flies are shown on a dead plant and a dead animal, helping break them down. Nearby, a small bird and another animal are shown eating fly eggs and young, showing that flies and their young are food for other animals.

pages.text: Gross but Cool! Flies are amazing insects!
pages.brief: Several flies are shown together on a leaf, some resting with wings spread and some walking on their thin legs. They look busy and alive in warm light, showing that flies are amazing insects, even though they can seem gross.

books.title: Hedgehogs
books.art_why: Hedgehogs are real animals that can be photographed.

pages.text: What Are Hedgehogs? Hedgehogs are mammals. They have sharp quills on their backs.
pages.brief: A single hedgehog stands in view, showing its small face and body and the sharp quills covering its back. The quills are clearly visible across the animal's back, showing the hedgehog as a mammal with sharp quills.

pages.text: Stay Away! Hedgehogs roll themselves into a ball when they are scared. Their sharp quills stick out to keep other animals away.
pages.brief: A hedgehog is rolled tightly into a ball in a defensive pose, its sharp quills sticking out all around it. It has rolled up because it is scared, and the quills point outward to keep other animals away.

pages.text: Bodies and Senses Hedgehogs have short legs and short tails.
pages.brief: A hedgehog is shown from the side so its body is clear. Its short legs are visible beneath it, and its short tail can be seen at the back. The picture focuses on the hedgehog's body and these two features.

pages.text: Hedgehogs have eyes, but they do not see well. They can hear and smell very well.
pages.brief: A close view of a hedgehog's face shows its eyes, ears and nose. The hedgehog's eyes are open, while its ears and nose are visible for hearing and smelling. The picture focuses on these senses.

pages.text: Why Are They Called That? Hedgehogs look under grass and bushes for food. They also make sounds like little hogs.
pages.brief: A hedgehog is shown with its snout under grass and bushes, searching for food. Its body is low to the ground among the plants. The scene shows where hedgehogs look for food and why they are linked with little hog sounds.

pages.text: What Do They Eat? Hedgehogs eat insects and worms. They also eat spiders, snails, slugs, frogs, toads, lizards, and snakes.
pages.brief: A hedgehog is shown near a group of animals it eats: insects, worms, a spider, a snail, a slug, a frog, a toad, a lizard and a snake. The hedgehog looks toward the food creatures around it.

pages.text: Night Animals Hedgehogs do most things at night. They sleep most of the day.
pages.brief: A hedgehog is shown awake and moving at night under a dark sky. Nearby, the same hedgehog is shown curled up asleep during the day. The scene contrasts the hedgehog being active at night with sleeping through most of the day.

pages.text: Most hedgehogs roll up in a ball when they sleep.
pages.brief: A hedgehog is curled tightly into a ball as it sleeps. Its body is round, with its head and short legs tucked in. The picture shows the rolled-up sleeping position that most hedgehogs use when they rest.

pages.text: Digging Animals Many hedgehogs live in burrows they dig with their front feet. Hedgehogs sometimes live in burrows dug by hares or foxes.
pages.brief: A hedgehog digs into the ground with its front feet, making a burrow. The burrow opening is visible in the soil. Nearby, another burrow opening is shown as a place hedgehogs sometimes live when hares or foxes have dug it.

pages.text: Where Do They Live? Hedgehogs live in Europe, Asia, and Africa. They were brought to New Zealand, and now some live there, too.
pages.brief: A large world map shows the areas of Europe, Asia, Africa and New Zealand. Small hedgehog figures stand on each area, showing where hedgehogs live and where they were brought. The map uses only land shapes and the hedgehog figures.

pages.text: Leave Me Alone! Hedgehogs live alone for most of their lives. They only live together to have more hedgehogs.
pages.brief: A single hedgehog is shown alone, with no other hedgehogs nearby. The picture shows the hedgehog living by itself for most of its life. In a separate small view, two hedgehogs are shown together only for the purpose of having more hedgehogs.

pages.text: Hedgehogs are funny little animals!
pages.brief: A hedgehog is shown as a funny little animal, with its small body and quills in clear view. Its pose makes it look lively and appealing. The picture presents the hedgehog as an amusing little creature.

books.title: Our Sun
books.art_why: The Sun, Earth, water, plants, weather, and sun safety are real-world subjects that can be photographed.

pages.text: Our Sun.
pages.brief: A large, bright Sun glowing in a wide sky, with warm rays spreading outward. The Sun is the only object shown, centered and clear, inviting a first look at the star that lights our world.

pages.text: What Is the Sun? The Sun is a star. A star is a large ball of gas that gives off energy. The Sun is the closest star to Earth.
pages.brief: A huge glowing ball of gas representing the Sun, with energy radiating outward. Beside it, far away, is a small Earth to show distance. The Sun appears as the closest star, a bright sphere in space.

pages.text: The Sun’s Energy We can feel the Sun’s energy as heat. We can see the Sun’s energy as light. Without heat and light, there would be no life on Earth.
pages.brief: The Sun shines above Earth, sending visible light and warmth toward the planet. On Earth’s surface, green plants and blue oceans are bright in sunlight. The scene shows heat and light reaching the land, suggesting life depends on them.

pages.text: Heat from the Sun Without the Sun’s heat, Earth would be too cold. The Sun warms Earth’s land, air, and oceans. Without the Sun’s heat, water would be solid ice.
pages.brief: The Sun’s warm rays reach Earth, touching land, air, and ocean. Below the glowing light, an ocean surface and rocky land look warmed, while a patch of water turns to solid ice in a cold, shadowed area to show what would happen without heat.

pages.text: The Sun’s heat turns ice to liquid water we can drink. All plants and animals need to drink water to live.
pages.brief: A block of ice melts into clear liquid water under the Sun’s warm rays. Nearby, a green plant and a small animal drink from a puddle of liquid water. The scene shows heat changing ice to water that living things need.

pages.text: Light from the Sun Without the Sun’s light, Earth would be dark. We need the Sun’s light to see.
pages.brief: The Sun shines brightly in space, sending light toward Earth. One side of Earth is lit and clear, while the other side is dark, with no detail visible. The bright sunlight lets the lit side be seen.

pages.text: The Sun’s light also helps plants grow. Plants use sunlight to make their own food. Humans and other animals need plants to live.
pages.brief: Green plants stand in bright sunlight, their leaves spread to catch the light as they make their own food. A human and a small animal are nearby, showing that people and animals need plants to live.

pages.text: The Sun and Weather Without the Sun, there would be no weather. The Sun’s heat turns liquid water to gas.
pages.brief: The Sun shines over a body of liquid water. Warm rays hit the water surface, and thin wisps of gas rise upward from the water into the air. The scene shows the Sun’s heat turning liquid water into gas.

pages.text: The gas rises into the air. When gas in the air gets cold, it turns into clouds.
pages.brief: Thin gas rises from water into the sky. Higher in the cooler air, the gas gathers and changes into soft white clouds against a pale blue background. The sky shows the gas cooling and forming clouds above the water.

pages.text: Clouds are made of tiny drops of water. When the drops get bigger, they fall as rain, snow, or hail.
pages.brief: A cloud hangs in the sky, made of many tiny water drops. Inside the cloud, small drops merge and grow larger. From the cloud, rain, snow, and hail fall down toward the ground below, showing different kinds of weather.

pages.text: The Sun Is Important Without the Sun’s heat, we would have no water or weather.
pages.brief: The Sun shines over Earth, warming the land and water. Below, liquid water and soft clouds show the water and weather the Sun makes possible. Without the Sun’s heat, the scene would have no water or weather.

pages.text: Without the Sun’s light, we would have no plants or food. We need the Sun to live on Earth.
pages.brief: The Sun shines brightly above Earth, sending light to green plants growing in soil. A human stands near the plants, showing that people need plants for food. The scene shows that life on Earth needs the Sun.

pages.text: Sun Safety Too much light and heat from the Sun can hurt your eyes and skin. To stay safe when you play outside, follow these rules: • Never look directly at the Sun. • Wear sunglasses and sunscreen. • Stay in the shade. • Drink plenty of water.
pages.brief: Children play outside under a bright Sun. One child wears sunglasses and sunscreen, another stands in the shade, and a water bottle is nearby. No one looks directly at the Sun, showing safe ways to enjoy sunny weather.

books.title: Ships and Boats
books.art_why: Real ships, boats, harbours and modern craft exist today and can be photographed, including museum replicas of early boats.

pages.text: Introduction Ships and boats are part of human history. They were once the fastest way to travel.
pages.brief: A wide harbour of calm blue water filled with ships and boats of many sizes, from small open craft to tall vessels, some under way carrying travellers across the water, showing the boats people have long relied on to move from place to place.

pages.text: Early Ships and Boats The first boats were made out of logs. People used poles to push the boats.
pages.brief: Two people stand on a floating log boat in shallow river water, each gripping a long wooden pole and pressing it down into the riverbed to push the rough log slowly forward, the earliest kind of boat afloat.

pages.text: Other boats used paddles or oars. The oars pushed against the water to move the boats.
pages.brief: A person kneels low in a wooden boat on a calm lake, both hands on a wooden paddle, the blade dipped into the water and pulling back hard, pushing against the water to drive the small boat along.

pages.text: Later, people made boats with wooden frames. They covered the frames with bark or animal skins.
pages.brief: On a grassy riverbank, a boat builder bends a wooden frame of curved branches and stretches bark and animal skins over it, lashing the covering tight, the half-finished frame boat resting on the ground near the water's edge.

pages.text: Frame boats were larger than log boats. Many people could row at the same time.
pages.brief: A long frame boat sits on the water with rows of people seated along both sides, each holding an oar, pulling together in time as the wide hull carries many passengers across the river at once.

pages.text: Sails were used to move boats, too. The sails caught the wind to push the boat.
pages.brief: A boat on open water with a cloth sail hoisted on a mast, the sail bellied out and full as the wind catches it and pushes the boat forward, ripples sliding past the wooden hull.

pages.text: Larger ships needed more sails. Sailing ships carried people around the world.
pages.brief: A large sailing ship with several tall masts and many billowing sails crosses open sea, crew and passengers on deck, a distant coastline behind, the ship carrying people on long voyages around the world.

pages.text: Modern Ships and Boats Many ships and boats today are made of metal or plastic. They often use engines to move through the water.
pages.brief: On a wide bay, a modern metal boat moves across the water with an engine turning at the stern and a white wake churning behind, while a plastic-hulled boat nearby glides past under engine power instead of oars.

pages.text: Some boats do special jobs. Tugboats push and pull larger ships. Ferryboats carry cars and people. Fireboats put out fires on other ships.
pages.brief: A busy harbour: a small tugboat presses its padded bow against a huge ship to push it; a ferryboat loaded with cars and people crosses to a far dock; a fireboat sends a high arc of water onto a burning ship.

pages.text: Many countries use ships and boats to help defend them.
pages.brief: A grey navy ship patrols open sea under a wide sky, flag flying, sailors standing watch along the deck and scanning the horizon, one of the ships countries use to help defend their coasts and home waters.

pages.text: People still use smaller boats for fishing and fun. Many small boats still use paddles or oars.
pages.brief: A small rowboat on a quiet lake with an adult and a child leaning over the side with fishing lines, while nearby another small boat is paddled for fun, oars and paddle blades dipping into the water.

pages.text: Conclusion Ships and boats are still an important part of our world.
pages.brief: A wide river mouth at sunset with many kinds of boats on the water, a rowboat, a sailing boat and a working boat, all still moving and at work, showing that ships and boats remain an important part of our world.

books.title: Spring Is Here
books.art_why: Real-world spring nature can be photographed.

pages.text: The Warmer Days of Spring Remember how the sun feels on the first warm day of spring? In spring, each day grows longer and warmer.
pages.brief: A bright sun shines in an open spring sky over an outdoor landscape, casting warm light on the ground and trees. The days are growing longer and warmer, and the scene feels mild and bright after winter.

pages.text: The plants and animals feel it grow warmer, too.
pages.brief: Plants and animals in a spring outdoor setting feel the warmer air. Green plants stand in the mild sunshine while small creatures move about outdoors, showing that living things notice the rising temperature around them.

pages.text: The Garden The flowers send up shoots from round white bulbs. Soon the garden will be filled with color.
pages.brief: In a garden, round white bulbs sit in the soil and send up green shoots. Small plants are beginning to grow, and the garden will soon be filled with bright color as spring flowers develop.

pages.text: The robins are back at work. They collect brown grass for a nest. Soon they will feed wiggly worms to hungry babies.
pages.brief: Two robins are back at work outdoors in a yard, busy collecting brown grass for a nest. Wiggly worms nearby suggest the small food they will soon feed to little hungry babies in the nest.

pages.text: The Woods The trees are growing again. The fat buds on a tree grow into big, flat leaves. Caterpillars nibble on them.
pages.brief: In the woods, trees are growing again in spring. Fat buds on a tree open into big, flat green leaves, and small caterpillars nibble on the young green leaves among the woodland branches all around.

pages.text: The cricket comes out from It rubs its wings to make the sound “chirp, chirp.”
pages.brief: A small cricket comes out in the woods and rubs its wings together to make a chirping sound. It is active near the ground among the little spring plants and grass as it moves about.

pages.text: The Mountains In the mountains, snow melts away. Streams fill with water.
pages.brief: In the mountains, snow melts away under the bright warmer spring sun. Water runs down the slopes, and streams fill with cold mountain meltwater, flowing through the open rocky landscape as the winter ice disappears.

pages.text: The bear comes out from her underground den. She is hungry.
pages.brief: A bear comes out from her underground den in the mountains. She stands quietly outside near the den entrance in the spring air, looking hungry after her long cold winter rest in the dark den.

pages.text: The Meadow A baby deer drinks its mother’s milk. Soon it will eat soft spring grass.
pages.brief: In a green meadow, a small baby deer drinks its mother’s milk. The mother stands quietly close by, and soft spring grass grows all around them in the open meadow under the warm spring sun.

pages.text: Gophers kick up piles of brown soil. They nibble on dandelion leaves.
pages.brief: Small gophers are busy digging in a meadow, kicking up piles of brown soil around their burrows. They nibble on green dandelion leaves growing nearby in the soft spring grass of the open meadow outdoors.

pages.text: The Pond It’s also warmer at the pond. The turtles lie on a log in the sun.
pages.brief: At a calm open pond, warmer spring weather brings several turtles onto a log. They lie in the sun on the log at the water’s edge, resting in the bright spring light near the pond.

pages.brief: On a calm quiet pond, a water lily’s flat, round green leaf lies on top of the water. A small frog sits on the leaf, looking out with its mouth open wide as spring arrives.
